strengths: Identifies and clearly characterizes a novel and practically important failure mode ('sink trap') in native text-to-3D generative models, where text conditioning becomes insensitive to out-of-distribution prompts while the model retains rich geometric expressivity -- a useful diagnostic contribution for the 3D generative modeling community.

The proposed fix is simple, well-motivated, and elegant: perform inversion with an empty/null prompt plus null-text optimization to stabilize sampling trajectories, then edit purely by resampling with the target text embedding, without any auxiliary masks, multi-view 2D priors, or image inpainting models, unlike prior 3D editing pipelines.

Solid supporting analysis: SigLIP-based diversity ratio study (Table 1, Fig. 2) quantifying non-uniform semantic coverage, and velocity-norm/L1 reconstruction studies (Table 2, Fig. 4, Fig. 6) that convincingly show approximate prompts destabilize inversion in TRELLIS but not in 2D diffusion/flow models (FLUX, Stable Diffusion), reinforcing the paper's core claim of a 3D-specific phenomenon.

Favorable comparisons against relevant recent baselines (VoxHammer, native TRELLIS second-stage editing) on the DT4D non-rigid shape benchmark, showing both qualitative superiority (geometry-level edits vs. texture-only changes) and large efficiency gains (~20x speedup, no manual masking).

Good transparency about limitations: the paper explicitly shows and discusses failure cases on extreme out-of-distribution poses (Fig. 9), rather than hiding them, and proposes reasonable future directions.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed algorithm pseudocode (Alg. 1) and dataset construction details are provided in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: All experiments rely on a single 3D generative backbone (TRELLIS); the newer TRELLIS.2 is excluded on relevance grounds, so it remains unclear whether the 'sink trap' phenomenon and the proposed fix generalize across other native text-to-3D architectures/backbones.

The quantitative editing evaluation is fairly thin: Table 3 reports a single SigLIP alignment score on essentially one dataset/setting, with no user study or additional perceptual/geometric-plausibility metrics to corroborate that edits are semantically faithful and not just superficially well-aligned in embedding space.

No quantitative comparison against other recent text-driven 3D editing approaches referenced in related work (e.g., Nano3D, 3D-Latte), only against VoxHammer and TRELLIS's native pipeline, limiting the breadth of the empirical case for state-of-the-art status.

The 'expressivity mismatch' framing could be partially confounded with standard training-data distribution effects (i.e., certain semantic categories being underrepresented in the text-to-3D training data) rather than a fundamentally distinct decoupling of geometric vs. linguistic capacity; the paper does not fully rule out this alternative explanation.

The frequency/severity of the acknowledged failure mode (edits on geometrically OOD poses, Fig. 9) is not quantified, making it hard to assess how often practitioners would encounter unreliable edits.
Evaluation datasets are modest in scale (80 TRELLIS-generated shapes, 208 DT4D frames from 13 sequences), which somewhat limits the statistical strength of the quantitative claims.

strengths: Identifies and clearly characterizes a novel and important failure mode in native text-to-3D generative models ("sink trap"), where diverse out-of-distribution prompts collapse to near-identical geometries; this is a valuable diagnostic contribution not previously documented in the 3D generative modeling literature.

The diversity-ratio metric (Δvis/Δtxt using SigLIP) is a reasonable and reproducible way to quantify the language-geometry mismatch, and the authors validate the phenomenon across three different 3D generative backbones (TRELLIS, LN3Diff, GaussianAnything), strengthening the generality of the observation.

The proposed fix (empty-prompt Euler inversion + null-text optimization) is simple, well-motivated by the velocity-norm/CFG instability analysis, and is shown to substantially improve reconstruction (L1/LPIPS) over approximate-prompt inversion and over the standard NTI baseline on non-rigid DT4D shapes.

The resulting editing pipeline is compared against multiple strong/relevant baselines (VoxHammer, TRELLIS native second-stage editing, Vox-E, Instant3DiT) with both quantitative (SigLIP/CLIP/VLM scores) and qualitative results, and shows clear advantages in geometric retargeting fidelity while being far more computationally efficient (~9s/edit vs. >1 hour for Vox-E) and mask-free unlike VoxHammer/Instant3DiT.

The paper extends the analysis to 2D T2I models (FLUX, Stable Diffusion, COCO/DiffusionDB) to contrast behavior, providing useful context that the sink-trap instability is comparatively more severe in native 3D generative latent spaces than in mature 2D diffusion models.

Reasonably thorough supplementary material (algorithm pseudocode, dataset construction details, additional qualitative figures) supports reproducibility, and limitations (failure on highly OOD poses, lack of explicit plausibility constraints) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: it largely amounts to substituting an approximate source prompt with an empty/null prompt within existing Euler inversion + NTI machinery (already established in the 2D domain), rather than a fundamentally new mechanism tailored to 3D flow latents.

The full editing pipeline and quantitative editing evaluations (Table 3, Fig. 7-9) are demonstrated only on TRELLIS; the multi-model generality claim is supported only by the diversity-ratio analysis (Table 1) for LN3Diff and GaussianAnything, not by the actual inversion/editing experiments, leaving open whether the proposed fix generalizes to other backbones.

VLM-based evaluation relies on LLaVA-1.5-7B, a relatively dated and weaker VLM by current standards, which may add noise or bias to the reported editing-quality scores; no human study or stronger/more recent VLM judge is used to corroborate results.

Structural fidelity is not guaranteed: as acknowledged in Fig. 9 and the limitations section, edits on rare/OOD poses can produce implausible geometries since the method does not explicitly enforce geometric plausibility, somewhat undercutting the robustness claims made elsewhere in the paper.

Some comparisons are qualitative only or explicitly excluded from quantitative tables (e.g., "3D-latte" is mentioned in related work but not benchmarked; full-scene editing methods are excluded from Table 3 "for fairness"), which narrows the empirical comparison set and could understate the competitiveness of alternative approaches.

The efficiency claim (~9s per edit) is stated without full detail on how NTI's 10 inner optimization steps over 50 timesteps achieves this speed, and hardware/timing methodology could be more explicitly documented for reproducibility.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly characterized 'sink trap' phenomenon: the paper provides a compelling quantitative (SigLIP-based diversity ratio R) and qualitative (Fig. 2, Table 1) demonstration that text-to-3D models like TRELLIS, LN3Diff, and GaussianAnything collapse to near-identical geometries for out-of-distribution prompts, despite retaining the geometric capacity to represent diverse shapes.

The core insight—that combining an empty/null conditioning prompt with null-text optimization stabilizes inversion trajectories and unlocks the model's unconditional geometric prior—is simple, well-supported by velocity-norm analysis (Fig. 4), and effectively decouples geometric expressivity from linguistic sensitivity, a genuinely useful diagnostic and practical fix.

Strong empirical validation across multiple axes: reconstruction quality (L1, LPIPS) comparisons across prompt types and inversion methods (Table 2, Table 4), downstream editing quality via SigLIP/CLIP/VLM scores against several strong baselines (VoxHammer, Vox-E, Instant3DiT, native TRELLIS editing) with consistent improvements (Table 3), and cross-domain confirmation that the same prompt-insensitivity trend is much weaker in 2D T2I models (FLUX, SD) via matched experiments (Sec. F, Table 5), which strengthens the causal story that this is a 3D-specific issue.

Practical advantages are demonstrated, including large efficiency gains (~9s/edit) over slower baselines (Vox-E >1hr, VoxHammer needing manual masks and 150+ rendered views), and multiview-consistent 3D-native edits (Fig. 8) without requiring 2D priors, masks, or auxiliary image-based guidance—addressing a real gap identified in related work.

Honest limitations section (Fig. 9) showing failure cases on highly out-of-distribution poses, plus a thorough supplementary material with algorithm pseudocode (Alg. 1), dataset preparation details, and extensive additional qualitative results supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method and empirical validation are anchored almost entirely to TRELLIS's first-stage sparse structure model; the second-stage refinement (texture/SLAT) is kept fixed throughout, and no experiments generalize the full editing pipeline to other 3D generative backbones (LN3Diff/GaussianAnything are used only for the diversity analysis, not for editing/inversion validation), leaving open how well the proposed inversion+editing recipe transfers beyond one architecture.

Editing quality evaluation relies substantially on automatic proxies (SigLIP/CLIP similarity, LLaVA-1.5-7B scoring with a self-defined 1-5 rubric) without a human user study, which is a comparatively weak evidence source for subjective notions like editing plausibility and prompt fidelity.

The comparison with VoxHammer may be somewhat imbalanced: it fails on 67% of DT4D samples due to latent-value explosion, and it also requires manual 3D masks, which are structurally different requirements than the proposed method's; while the paper appropriately notes these differences, the quantitative gap partly reflects this mismatch rather than a purely like-for-like editing-quality comparison.

The diversity ratio R (Sec. 4.1) is a useful heuristic but is based on cosine similarity in a non-metric embedding space and is not validated against any ground-truth notion of geometric diversity (e.g., correlation with human judgments or explicit shape-space distances), so its precision as a measure of 'sink trap' severity is somewhat informal.

Failure cases (Fig. 9) are shown only qualitatively; there is no quantitative characterization of how often or under what conditions the editing pipeline becomes unstable for rare/OOD poses, which would help readers gauge the practical reliability of the method.

The computational cost accounting (9s/edit) is not clearly broken out to include the null-text inversion cost (50 steps × 10 inner Adam iterations), which could be a substantial overhead not fully reflected in the reported efficiency comparison.
